evaluations.rationale: This answer chooses the 20-megawatt incremental-cost floor and defends that choice with assignment-specific distinctions, not a generic cost-causation slogan. It correctly separates Section 2107(a), which would force FERC within 270 days to rewrite the October 26, 1994 Transmission Pricing Policy Statement so computational loads pay embedded and incremental transmission costs with no megawatt cutoff, from Section 2107(b), which would add Federal Power Act section 228 for covered loads of 20 megawatts or more, including phased and commonly controlled multi-site loads. Those statutory features match the introduced September 30, 2026 text as analyzed by Foley Hoag. The answer also correctly treats the floor as a minimum covering generation, storage, transmission, and distribution, with financial assurances, continued recovery if the load exits, and preserved state tools such as open seasons and bring-your-own generation. Its account of the 1994 policy is accurate: FERC rejected postage-stamp “and” pricing as unjust and unreasonable because embedded and incremental charges were alternative measures of the same transmission capacity, and it allowed the higher of the two. The roughly two-and-a-half-year implementation lag is also supported, because Foley Hoag notes a revised policy within 270 days, a proposed rule within 270 days after that, and a final rule within a further year. The Peskoe counterargument is fairly stated. His April 15, 2026 Utility Dive essay does argue that the 1994 ban was aimed at utilities overcharging competing generators, not at subsidizing new consumers, and that a narrow “higher of” reading can leave either network or upgrade costs on everyone else. Grid Strategies’ November 2, 2026 paper does estimate about $55 billion over ten years under the rewrite, about $35 billion more than current policy, on about 40.3 gigawatts outside ERCOT assuming firm service. The answer’s claim that the $136 billion figure is an upper bound if states use the floor is directionally right, though TechTarget reports it more narrowly as incremental generation costs under full state implementation, not simply “broader costs.” That compression does not undermine the reasoning. The decisive strength is that the answer does not pretend the floor automatically collects embedded transmission charges. It argues that states and FERC may charge more than incremental cost and credit the surplus, while refusing to lock stacked transmission pricing into the just-and-reasonable standard for every computational site. That is a coherent response to the forced choice, including the prior selected answer’s preference for a separable 20-megawatt cost floor.

This answer also demonstrates genuine, assignment-specific reasoning and should not be treated as failing Proof of Reasoning merely because it reaches the opposite conclusion. It accurately identifies the October 26, 1994 policy, published November 3, 1994, at 59 Federal Register 55031, and correctly states that FERC treated charging both an embedded-cost rate and an incremental-cost rate for the same service over the same facilities as unjust and unreasonable, with the lawful charge the higher of the two. It fairly reports Peskoe’s April 2026 Utility Dive argument that embedded costs are a contribution to the shared network and incremental costs are facilities the load causes. Its Grid Strategies figures are also reliable: about $55 billion over ten years, roughly $35 billion embedded and $20 billion incremental, about $35 billion more than current policy, for about 40.3 gigawatts outside ERCOT, excluding off-grid projects, with the $136 billion figure an upper bound rather than a forecast. The answer is especially careful that those figures are assumptions, not statutory findings. Its core argument—that only the size-neutral rewrite prices use of the existing network plus new facilities, while the floor by itself does not compel an embedded-cost contribution—is a real and well-supported distinction. It also correctly notes the revenue-requirement credit, the lower non-firm rate, and the risk that a 20-megawatt cutoff can invite project splitting, though the bill’s phased and commonly controlled aggregation reduces that risk more than the answer acknowledges. The ranking is lower because the answer overstates what Congress would be choosing. It says the floor “does not, by itself, make a large load pay its share of the embedded grid,” which is true of the statutory minimum, but it underweights the bill’s express authority for FERC or a state to charge more than incremental cost and credit the surplus, including above embedded average cost. It also treats the credit as a complete answer to double-counting, whereas rolled-in embedded rates already contain prior expansions, so the overlap problem is harder than the answer allows. Calling the floor “partly state-implemented” is fair as to the $136 billion generation scenario, but the no-shift rule itself would be a federal floor, not merely an optional state program. Those are comparative weaknesses, not a failure of effort.

rationale: Both candidates meet Proof of Reasoning. Each chooses one of the two governing rules the question forces, distinguishes Section 2107(a)’s size-neutral rewrite of FERC’s 1994 transmission pricing policy from Section 2107(b)’s 20-megawatt Federal Power Act floor, engages the strongest opposing argument, and uses the Grid Strategies estimates as assumptions rather than statutory facts. Independent checks confirm the shared premises: the policy statement was issued October 26, 1994, and published November 3, 1994, at 59 FR 55031; it rejected “and” pricing for the same service over the same facilities and allowed the higher of embedded or incremental cost; Peskoe’s April 15, 2026 Utility Dive essay argues that premise does not fit data-center loads; and Grid Strategies’ November 2, 2026 paper estimates about $55 billion over ten years under the rewrite, about $35 billion more than current policy, on about 40.3 gigawatts outside ERCOT, with about $136 billion as a separate upper-bound generation figure if states fully use the floor. Candidate-01 ranks first because it more precisely tracks the introduced bill’s minimum-not-cap structure, financial assurances, continued recovery, and state tools, and because it answers the forced choice without claiming the floor already solves embedded-cost recovery. Candidate-02 is factually careful and makes the stronger case that the floor’s statutory minimum leaves embedded transmission charges unassigned, but it overreads the revenue-requirement credit and underweights the bill’s authority to charge above incremental and embedded average cost. Neither disagreement nor those comparative errors justifies meetsPor=false.
